name: Web-Shooters
summary: Peter Parker's homemade wrist launchers fire a sticky fluid he cooked up himself. Swinging between skyscrapers is his power; the webs are pure teenage chemistry.

parts.label: Housing
parts.fact: In the comics Peter builds the wrist units himself. Steve Ditko's design notes show he chose a hidden wrist device over the idea of a web gun carried in a holster.

parts.label: Web fluid
parts.fact: In the comics the fluid stays nearly solid until it is forced through the nozzle, is chemically related to nylon, and breaks down into dust after about an hour.

parts.label: Nozzle modes
parts.fact: On film, the Stark-made suit in Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017) boasts 576 web combinations, from taser webs to web grenades, picked by hand gesture or voice.

parts.label: Palm trigger
parts.fact: In the comics the trigger sits flat in the palm and needs a quick double tap from the middle and ring fingers, plus heavy pressure, so a clenched fist never fires it.

parts.label: Wrist band
parts.fact: On film, Sam Raimi's Spider-Man (2002) dropped the bands entirely and gave Peter organic webs. The Amazing Spider-Man (2012) brought the mechanical bands back.

trivia: Raimi did not skip mechanical shooters lightly: props were made and some shots were filmed with them before organic webs won out.
Screenwriter David Koepp has credited the organic-web idea to James Cameron, who once developed his own Spider-Man film.
Artist Eric Stanton, who shared a studio with Ditko, claimed he suggested having the webs shoot from Spidey's hands.
The Homecoming suit's AI, Karen, is voiced by Jennifer Connelly.
